description: We are RIM Team from Mauritania , taking on the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge. Our goal is to bring back to life the stories of NASA's equipment left on the Moon and Mars through an interactive storytelling website. We combine research, design and web development, and we work in French, English and Arabic
summary: Still Out There is a scroll-driven 3D journey to ten machines NASA left behind: Surveyor 3, Eagle, the Lunar Roving Vehicle and the Apollo 14 laser mirror on the Moon; Sojourner, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity on Mars; Kepler and Pioneer 10 in deep space. As you scroll, you fly from Earth at the real light-travel time and land beside each machine at its real coordinates, lit by the Sun exactly as it is right now. Every stop answers three questions: what the machine was, why it went silent, and what it taught us. Tap a machine for its real NASA photo, or play "Can you spot it?" and find it in the orbital image of where it lies today. Real NASA recordings carry the big moments, from Eagle's lift-off countdown to the wind on Mars, and each machine tells its own story in English, French and Arabic. We built it so students see this hardware as a record of what we learned, not as junk. Every fact is sourced, and anything we simplified is labelled.
details:
What it does Still Out There is one continuous 3D universe that the scroll drives. You leave Earth, and a clock counts the real light-travel time as the camera flies to the Moon, then Mars, then deep space. At each of 18 stops the camera lands beside a machine at its real latitude and longitude, and a card builds: what it was, why it went silent, what it taught us. Scrolling back rewinds everything.

Highlights:

  • Lit as it is right now. Earth, the Moon and Mars are turned so today's sunlit side faces the Sun. If it is night at Eagle's landing site, the close-up is dark. The Sun angle at every site matches NASA's Mars24 algorithm and Astronomy Engine to 0.1°.
  • Eagle's lift-off. Only the bottom half of Eagle is on the Moon. Its top half lifts off to the real Apollo 11 onboard recording of Aldrin's countdown, with captions from the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal.
  • The dust storm. At Opportunity the sky darkens as the 2018 storm's dust opacity rises from tau 0.5 to 10.8, the two real readings, until the rover's last call home.
  • The echo. At the Apollo 14 mirror you fire a laser at the Moon and wait the real round-trip time for the reflection.
  • Can you spot it? For Eagle, the lunar rover, the Apollo 14 mirror and InSight, you look for the machine in the real LRO or HiRISE orbital photo (with NASA's labels painted out), see how many metres off you were, then see NASA's labelled original.
  • Real sounds. InSight's marsquake, Ingenuity's flight heard by Perseverance, the wind on Mars, and Perseverance's hum on the way there.
  • Stories. Each machine tells a five-chapter story in its own voice, in English, French and Arabic. Each sentence lights up as it is read, and each chapter has a "Real data" drawer with the sourced facts.
  • Roll call. The journey ends at an Earthrise, where all ten machines answer in turn.

Benefits and intended impact Most people know the famous missions but not what was left behind, or why it still matters. Each machine is tied to one discovery, so the science sticks: the Apollo 14 mirror still measures the Moon's distance to within a few millimetres; InSight heard 1,319 marsquakes that revealed the layers inside Mars; Kepler showed our galaxy has more planets than stars. A 2-minute self-playing tour gives a quick version for classrooms. Three languages, including Arabic and French, let it reach students in Mauritania, where we are from, and across North and West Africa. It runs in any modern browser on a phone or laptop with no install, and browsers without 3D get the same stops as a page of cards.

How it works and tools used Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step. three.js (WebGL) renders the scene; GSAP ties camera moves and animation to the scroll; Astronomy Engine and NASA's Mars24 algorithm compute live sunlight and local time at each site; JPL Horizons gives the live distances to Kepler and Pioneer 10. Sound is mixed live from the scroll position with the Web Audio API. Six machines are NASA 3D Resources models; NASA has no public model of Surveyor 3, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, the laser mirror or Sojourner, so we built simplified models in code from NASA photos and published sizes, and each card says so. Assets were prepared with Python, ffmpeg and glTF-Transform, and the site is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Automated tests check the time engines against published reference values and refuse any fact without a source.

How it is creative Scrolling is the spaceship: one gesture flies you between worlds, lands you and rewinds you. Time is real: the light clocks, the sunlight and the laser echo all run on today's actual geometry, so no two visits look the same. The orbital "spot it" game turns NASA's survey images into a puzzle, and letting each machine speak in the first person makes a 1967 lander something a 12-year-old wants to listen to.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty. 102 facts, each linked to one of 56 sources. Anything not to scale or simplified is labelled on screen: sizes and distances between worlds are compressed to fit, and the on-screen clocks give the real distances. Where NASA has published only the landing site (Opportunity, Ingenuity), the card says so.
  • Respect for NASA branding. No NASA logos, insignia or mission patches are used, and the site states it is not made or endorsed by NASA.
  • Access. Works on phones, has keyboard controls, captions for the lift-off audio, a readable font (Atkinson Hyperlegible) and a no-3D fallback. The site opens only when everything is downloaded (about 13 MB on desktop, less on phones), so it does not stall mid-flight.
